quote: I realized that once I could guess what my answer would be—once I could assign a higher probability to deciding one way than other—then I had, in all probability, already decided.
content: The underconfidence is the title's claim. Colleagues who put their chance of switching at about a third actually switched once in twenty-four times. They believed their minds were more open than they were: we change our minds less often than we think. Fable's alternative moral, "people know themselves better than they think," reports the same number and calls it self-knowledge. The essay reads it as a warning about how much the remaining deliberation can do. Fable's chess analogy supports that reading. If halfway through a game you could name the winner 96% of the time, the remaining moves would rarely change the result, and the essay's warning is about that small remainder of deliberation that still matters.

quote: Between hindsight bias, fake causality, positive bias, anchoring/priming, et cetera, et cetera, and above all the dreaded confirmation bias, once an idea gets into your head, it’s probably going to stay there.
content: Choice-blindness research adds evidence for the essay. Participants who were given a choice they had not made, and who argued for it, went on to prefer that option in later, unmanipulated choices (Johansson et al. 2014). A preference planted by sleight of hand, once defended, stayed. "Once an idea gets into your head, it's probably going to stay there," even when someone else put it there. Wood and Porter's corrections concern isolated facts. The essay concerns beliefs and decisions that people have already committed to. The date and hour of the author's own change of mind do not contradict the title, which is "less often than we think," not "never." A mind change memorable enough to be dated to the hour is a sign that it was rare.
